Features such as 'mean radius', 'mean perimeter', and 'mean area' are often correlated with tumor size and may appear more stable across benign and malignant cases. Moreover, 'mean fractal dimension' is more relevant to surface complexity and is typically higher in malignant cases, so low values may not be significant. Given the model predicted malignancy with high confidence, features that are not strong discriminators — such as those reflecting general size or smoothness — may have had minimal impact. Thus, these features are suspected to have minimal biological significance in distinguishing malignancy.

comparison.query: Compare the magnitude of the mean fractal dimension (0.06213) and mean smoothness (0.1054) in known malignant vs benign tumor profiles; which is more likely to influence malignancy?

findings.reasoning: In known malignant vs benign tumor profiles, mean smoothness is consistently more correlated with malignancy than mean fractal dimension. Malignant tumors typically exhibit higher irregularity and surface complexity, which translates into lower mean smoothness values. For example, in the Breast Cancer Wisconsin (Diagnostic) dataset, mean smoothness has a strong inverse relationship with malignancy — values below 0.11 are more frequently observed in malignant cases. In contrast, mean fractal dimension, while associated with surface complexity, shows a more subtle and less consistent signal across datasets. Specifically, mean smoothness has been statistically validated in multiple studies as a key differentiator in malignancy prediction, with higher predictive power in logistic regression and decision tree models. The current value of mean smoothness (0.1054) is on the lower end of the malignant spectrum, reinforcing its relevance. Meanwhile, mean fractal dimension (0.06213) is within the typical benign range and shows less discriminative power in clinical models.
